Then he brought the family groups of Benjamin near. The family group of Matri was chosen. Then Saul son of Kish was chosen. But when they looked for him, they could not find him.
So they asked the LORD, "Has the man come here?" The LORD said, "Yes. He is hiding among the supplies."
They ran and brought him out. When he stood among the people, he was taller than everyone else.
Then Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see the man the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people." Then all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"
Then Samuel told the people what a king should do. He wrote it in a book. He put the book before the LORD. Then he sent all the people home.
Saul went home to Gibeah too. Some brave men went with him. God had touched their hearts.
But some bad men said, "How can this man save us?" They did not like him. They did not bring him a gift. But Saul did not say anything.
Nahash was the king of the Ammonites. He went up and camped near Jabesh-gilead. The men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Make an agreement with us, and we will serve you.”
Nahash the Ammonite said to them, “I will make an agreement with you, but I must take out the right eye of every one of you. Then all of Israel will be ashamed.”
The leaders of Jabesh said to him, “Give us seven days. We will send messengers all over Israel. If no one comes to save us, we will come out to you.”
The messengers came to Gibeah, where Saul lived. They told the people the news. All the people cried out loud and wept.
Saul was coming in from the field behind his oxen. He asked, “Why are the people crying?” They told him what the men of Jabesh had said.
When Saul heard this, the Spirit of God came on him with power. He became very angry.

Saul took a pair of oxen and cut them into pieces. He sent the pieces by messengers all over Israel. He said, “This is what will happen to the oxen of anyone who does not follow Saul and Samuel into battle.” The fear of the LORD fell on the people, and they all came out together as one man.
Saul counted them at Bezek. There were 300,000 men from Israel and 30,000 men from Judah.
They told the messengers to tell the men of Jabesh-gilead, “Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will be saved.” The messengers went and told the men of Jabesh, and they were glad.
The men of Jabesh said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you can do to us whatever seems good to you.”

The next day Saul split the army into three groups. They attacked the Ammonite camp in the early morning. They fought until the sun was hot. The Ammonites who were left ran away. Not even two of them stayed together.
The people said to Samuel, “Who said, ‘Saul should not be our king’? Give us those men, and we will put them to death.”
Saul said, “No one will be put to death today, because today the LORD has saved Israel.”
Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and make Saul king again there.”
All the people went to Gilgal. There they made Saul king before the LORD. They offered peace offerings to the LORD. Saul and all the men of Israel were very happy there.
Samuel said to all Israel, “Look, I have listened to your voice in all you said to me, and I have set a king over you.
Now look, the king walks before you. I am old and gray. My sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until today.

Today, here I am. Tell me if I have done wrong before the LORD and before His anointed. Did I take anyone's ox? Did I take anyone's donkey? Did I cheat anyone? Did I hurt anyone? Did I take money from anyone to look the other way? Tell me, and I will give it back.”
“You have not cheated us,” they said. “You have not hurt us. You have not taken anything from anyone.”
Samuel said, “The LORD is a witness against you, and His anointed is a witness today. You have not found anything in my hand.” “He is a witness,” they said.
Samuel said to the people, “The LORD is the One who made Moses and Aaron. He brought your fathers up from Egypt.
Now stand here. I will judge you before the LORD. I will tell you all the good things the LORD did for you and your fathers.
When Jacob came to Egypt, your fathers cried to the LORD. The LORD sent Moses and Aaron. They brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place.
But they forgot the LORD their God. So He let their enemies beat them. He let Sisera, the army leader of Hazor, and the Philistines, and the king of Moab fight against them.
They cried to the LORD and said, “We have sinned. We left the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtoreths. Now save us from our enemies' hands, and we will serve You.”
Then the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel. He saved you from your enemies all around, and you lived in safety.
But when you saw Nahash king of the Ammonites coming against you, you said to me, “No, a king must rule over us,” even though the LORD your God was your king.
Now here is the king you chose, the one you asked for. See, the LORD has set a king over you.
If you fear the LORD and serve Him, and obey His voice, and do not go against the LORD's words, then you and your king will keep following the LORD your God.
But if you do not obey the LORD, and you rebel against the LORD, then the LORD's hand will be against you and your fathers.
Now stand and see this great thing the LORD will do before your eyes.
Today is wheat harvest time. I will pray to the LORD, and He will send thunder and rain. Then you will know and see that you did a very bad thing in the LORD's eyes when you asked for a king.
Samuel called to the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day. All the people were very afraid of the LORD and Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray to the LORD your God for us, your servants, so we will not die. We have added to all our sins by asking for a king.”
Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this wrong. But do not stop following the LORD. Serve the LORD with all your heart.
Do not chase empty things that cannot help you or save you. They are useless.
The LORD will not leave His people, because of His great name. It pleased the LORD to make you His people.
I would never sin against the LORD by stopping my prayers for you. I will teach you the good and right way.
But you must fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all your heart. Remember what great things He has done for you.
But if you keep doing wrong, you and your king will be destroyed.”
Saul was one year old when he became king. He ruled Israel for two years.

Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand stayed with Saul at Michmash and in the hills near Bethel. One thousand stayed with Jonathan in Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul sent the rest of the people home.
Jonathan attacked the Philistine camp at Geba. The Philistines heard about it. Saul blew a horn all over the land. He said, "Let the Hebrews hear this!"
All Israel heard the news. They said, "Saul attacked a Philistine camp. Now the Philistines hate Israel!" Then the people were called to join Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight Israel. They had thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and many soldiers. There were as many soldiers as sand on the seashore. They camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.
The men of Israel saw they were in trouble. Their army was weak. So they hid in caves, bushes, rocks, strong places, and holes in the ground.
Some Hebrews crossed the Jordan River. They went to the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed at Gilgal. All his soldiers were very scared.
Saul waited seven days for the time Samuel set. Samuel did not come to Gilgal. The soldiers began to leave Saul.
So Saul said, "Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings." Then he offered the burnt offering.
Just as Saul finished the burnt offering, Samuel came. Saul went out to meet him and greet him.
Samuel asked, "What have you done?" "I saw the soldiers leaving me. You did not come at the time you promised. The Philistines were gathering at Michmash.
I thought the Philistines would come down to fight me at Gilgal. I had not asked the LORD for help. So I felt I had to offer the burnt offering."
Samuel said, "You acted foolishly. You did not obey the command the LORD your God gave you. If you had obeyed, the LORD would have kept your kingdom strong forever.
But now your kingdom will not last. The LORD has found a man who wants to please Him. He has chosen that man to rule His people. This is because you did not obey the LORD's command."
Then Samuel got up and left Gilgal. He went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul counted the soldiers with him. There were about six hundred men.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the men with them stayed in Geba in Benjamin. The Philistines camped at Michmash.
The Philistines sent out soldiers to attack. They came in three groups. One group went toward Ophrah in the land of Shual.
Another group went toward Beth-horon. The third group went toward the border that looks over the Valley of Zeboim, toward the desert.
There was no metal worker in all Israel. The Philistines said, "The Hebrews must not make swords or spears."
So all Israel went down to the Philistines. They went to sharpen their plows, hoes, axes, and sickles.
They charged two-thirds of a shekel to sharpen plows, hoes, and forks. They charged one-third of a shekel to sharpen axes and fix goads.
So on the day of battle, none of the soldiers with Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear. Only Saul and Jonathan had them.
A group of Philistines went out to the mountain pass at Michmash.
One day Jonathan, Saul's son, said to the young man who carried his weapons, "Come, let's go over to the Philistines' guards on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
Saul was sitting under a pomegranate tree in Migron, at the edge of Gibeah. About six hundred men were with him.

Ahijah was wearing the special priest vest. He was the son of Ahitub, who was Ichabod's brother. Ahitub was the son of Phinehas, and Phinehas was the son of Eli, the priest of the LORD in Shiloh. The people did not know Jonathan had gone.
Between the passes Jonathan wanted to cross to the Philistines, there were sharp rocks on each side. One was called Bozez, and the other was called Seneh.
One rock stood to the north, across from Michmash. The other stood to the south, across from Geba.

Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come, let's go to the guards of these people who are not God's people. Maybe the LORD will help us. Nothing can stop the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few."
His helper said, "Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you. My heart is with your heart."
Jonathan said, "We will cross over to the men and show ourselves to them.
If they say, 'Stay there until we come to you,' then we will stand still and not go up to them.
But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for that will be our sign that the LORD has given them into our hands."
Both of them showed themselves to the Philistines' guards. The Philistines said, "Look! Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they were hiding."

The men at the guard post said to Jonathan and his helper, "Come up to us, and we will teach you a lesson." Jonathan said to his helper, "Follow me, for the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel."
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and his helper followed. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his helper killed them behind him.
In that first attack, Jonathan and his helper killed about twenty men in about half a field's length.
Then fear came on the camp, in the field, and among all the people. The guards and the attackers were afraid too. The ground shook. It was a very great fear sent by God.
Saul's watchmen in Gibeah of Benjamin saw the crowd melting away. They were going here and there.
Saul said to the people with him, "Count now and see who has gone from us." They counted, and Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.
Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God." For at that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.
While Saul was talking to the priest, the noise in the Philistines' camp kept getting louder and louder. Saul said to the priest, "Stop. Put your hand back."
Saul and all the people with him gathered and came to the battle. They saw that every Philistine had turned his sword against his friend. It was a very great confusion.
The Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before, and had gone up with them into the camp, turned to join the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
When all the men of Israel who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were running away, they also chased them in the battle.
So the LORD saved Israel that day. The battle passed beyond Beth-aven.

The men of Israel were worn out that day, for Saul had made the people promise, saying, "Cursed is the man who eats food before evening, before I have punished my enemies." So none of the people tasted food.
All the people came into the forest. There was honey on the ground.
When the people came into the forest, they saw honey dripping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, because the people feared the oath.

But Jonathan had not heard when his father made the people promise. He put out the end of the stick in his hand and dipped it into the honeycomb. He put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes became bright.
Then one of the people said, "Your father made the people promise, saying, 'Cursed is the man who eats food today.' That is why the people are so tired."
Jonathan said, "My father has brought trouble on the land. See how bright my eyes are because I tasted a little of this honey.
If only the people had eaten freely today from the things they took from their enemies! Then the killing of the Philistines would have been much greater."
That day they struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon. The people were very tired.
The people rushed on the spoil. They took sheep, cattle, and calves. They killed them on the ground and ate them with the blood still in them.
People told Saul, "Look, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating with the blood." Saul said, "You have broken faith. Roll a big stone to me today."

Saul said, "Go among the people and say, 'Each of you bring your ox or your sheep here. Kill them here and eat. Do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.'" So all the people brought their ox with their hand, and they killed it there.
Saul built an altar to the LORD. It was the first altar he built to the LORD.

Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night. Let us take their things until morning light. Let us not leave one of them." The people said, "Do whatever seems good to you." The priest said, "Let us go near to God here."
Saul asked God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will You give them into the hand of Israel?" But God did not answer him that day.
Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people. Find out and see how this sin happened today.
For as the LORD lives, who saves Israel, even if it is in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die." But none of the people answered him.
Then he said to all Israel, "You stand on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will stand on the other side." The people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you."
Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, "Give a clear answer." Saul and Jonathan were taken, but the people went free.
Saul said, "Draw lots between me and Jonathan my son." Jonathan was taken.
Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." Jonathan said, "I only tasted a little honey with the tip of the stick in my hand. Here I am. I am ready to die."
Saul said, "May God do so to me, and more, if you do not die, Jonathan."

The people said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die? He has brought this great victory to Israel. No! That must not happen! As the LORD lives, not one hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God today." So the people saved Jonathan, and he did not die.
Then Saul went up from following the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.

When Saul had taken the kingdom over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side: against Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he defeated them.
He fought bravely and struck down Amalek. He saved Israel from the hands of those who robbed them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His two daughters were named Merab, the older, and Michal, the younger.
Saul's wife was Ahinoam, the daughter of Ahimaaz. The leader of his army was Abner, the son of Ner, Saul's uncle.
Kish was Saul's father. Ner was Abner's father. Abiel was Ner's father.
There was hard fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. When Saul saw any strong or brave man, he took him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to pour oil on you and make you king over His people Israel. Now listen to what the LORD says.
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: 'I will punish the Amalekites for what they did to Israel. They attacked Israel on the way up from Egypt.'
Now go and attack the Amalekites. Destroy everything they have. Do not spare them. Kill men, women, children, and babies. Kill their oxen, sheep, camels, and donkeys."
So Saul called the people together. He counted them at Telaim. There were 200,000 foot soldiers and 10,000 men from Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek. He waited in the valley.
Saul said to the Kenites, "Leave now. Get away from the Amalekites. If you stay, I will destroy you with them. You were kind to Israel when they came up from Egypt." So the Kenites left.
Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur, near Egypt.
He caught Agag, king of the Amalekites, alive. He killed everyone else with swords.

But Saul and the people spared Agag. They also spared the best sheep, oxen, calves, and lambs. They spared everything good. They did not want to destroy those things. But they destroyed everything weak and worthless.
"I am sorry I made Saul king. He stopped following Me. He did not do what I told him." Samuel was very angry. He cried to the LORD all night.
Early in the morning, Samuel went to meet Saul. Someone told him, "Saul went to Carmel. He set up a monument there. Then he turned and went down to Gilgal."
Samuel came to Saul. Saul said, "The LORD bless you! I have done what the LORD told me."
Samuel said, "Then what is this sound of sheep and cows I hear?"
Saul said, "The people brought them from the Amalekites. They spared the best sheep and oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God. We destroyed the rest."
Samuel said, "Stop! Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night." "Speak," they said.
Samuel said, "You may think you are not important. But you are the leader of Israel's tribes. The LORD made you king over Israel.
The LORD sent you on a job. He said, 'Go and destroy the sinful Amalekites. Fight them until they are gone.'
Why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you take the things they had and do wrong in the eyes of the LORD?"
Saul said to Samuel, "But I did obey the LORD. I went where He sent me. I brought back Agag, king of Amalek. I destroyed the Amalekites.
But the people took some sheep and oxen from the things we were to destroy. They took the best ones to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal."
Samuel said, "Does The LORD want burnt offerings and sacrifices more than He wants you to obey Him? No. Obeying is better than sacrifice. Listening to Him is better than offering fat rams.
Rebelling is like the sin of witchcraft. Being stubborn is like worshiping false gods. You rejected the word of the LORD. So He rejected you as king."
Saul said to Samuel, "I sinned. I broke the command of the LORD and your words. I did it because I was afraid of the people. I listened to them instead.
Please forgive my sin now. Come back with me so I can worship the LORD."
Samuel said to Saul, "I will not go back with you. You rejected the word of the LORD. So the LORD rejected you as king over Israel."
As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the edge of his robe. It tore.
Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel away from you today. He has given it to someone better than you.
The LORD, the Glory of Israel, does not lie. He does not change His mind. He is not a man."
Then Saul said, "I sinned. But please honor me in front of my people's leaders and in front of Israel. Come back with me so I can worship the LORD your God."
So Samuel went back with Saul. Saul worshiped the LORD.
Samuel said, "Bring Agag, king of the Amalekites, to me." Agag came to him, looking cheerful. "Surely the worst of death is over."
Samuel said, "Your sword made many women lose their children. So your mother will lose her child." Then Samuel cut Agag into pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.
Samuel went to Ramah. Saul went up to his home in Gibeah.
Samuel never saw Saul again before Saul died. Samuel was very sad about Saul. The LORD was sorry He had made Saul king over Israel.

The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you be sad about Saul? I have said no to him being king over Israel. Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse in Bethlehem, for I have chosen one of his sons to be king."
Samuel said, "How can I go? Saul will hear about it and kill me." The LORD said, "Take a young cow with you. Say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.'"
The LORD said, "Then invite Jesse to the sacrifice. I will show you what to do. You are to put oil on the one I show you for Me."
Samuel did what the LORD said and went to Bethlehem. The city leaders met him. They were scared and asked, "Do you come in peace?"

"I have come in peace," Samuel replied. "I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Make yourselves clean and come with me to the sacrifice." Then he made Jesse and his sons clean and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and said, "Surely here before the LORD is His anointed."
But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look at how he looks or how tall he is. I have said no to him. People look at what is on the outside, but the LORD looks at the heart."
Then Jesse showed Abinadab to Samuel. Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Next Jesse showed Shammah to Samuel. Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Jesse showed seven of his sons to Samuel. Samuel said, "The LORD has not chosen any of these."
Samuel asked Jesse, "Are these all your sons?" Jesse replied, "There is still the youngest. He is taking care of the sheep." Samuel said, "Send for him. We will not sit down to eat until he comes."
So Jesse sent for him and brought him in. He was reddish, with beautiful eyes and a handsome face. The LORD said, "Rise and put oil on him, for he is the one."
Samuel took the horn of oil and put oil on David in front of his brothers. The Spirit of the LORD came on David with power from that day on. Then Samuel left and went to Ramah.
The Spirit of the LORD had left Saul. An evil spirit from the LORD began to trouble him.
Saul's servants said to him, "Surely an evil spirit from God is troubling you.
Let our master tell his servants here to find a man who can play the harp. He will play when the evil spirit from God comes on you, and you will feel better."
Saul said to his servants, "Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me."
One of the servants answered, "I have seen a son of Jesse in Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp. He is brave and strong, a fighter, speaks well, and is handsome. The LORD is with him."
Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me your son David, who is with the sheep."
Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat. He sent them to Saul with his son David.
David came to Saul and stood before him. Saul loved him very much. David became the one who carried Saul's armor.
Then Saul sent word to Jesse: "Let David stay with me, because I like him."
Whenever the spirit from God came on Saul, David took the harp and played. Saul felt better, and the evil spirit left him.
The Philistine people came together for war. They set up camp at Socoh in Judah. They camped between Socoh and Azekah at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel came together too. They set up camp in the Valley of Elah. They got ready to fight the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one hill. Israel stood on the other hill. The valley was between them.
A fighter named Goliath came out of the Philistine camp. He was from Gath. He was more than nine feet tall.
He wore a bronze helmet on his head. He wore bronze metal clothes. His metal clothes weighed about 125 pounds.
He wore bronze covers on his legs. He had a bronze small spear between his shoulders.
His spear was like a big weaving stick. Its iron point weighed about 15 pounds. A man carried his shield in front of him.
Goliath stood and shouted to the Israel army lines. He said, "Why do you come out to get ready for battle? I am a Philistine. You are Saul's servants. Pick one man and let him come down to me.
If he can fight me and kill me, we will be your servants. But if I beat him and kill him, you will be our servants and serve us."
Then the Philistine said, "I challenge the army lines of Israel today. Give me one man, and we will fight."
Saul and all Israel heard these words. They were very scared.
David was the son of Jesse. Jesse was from Bethlehem in Judah. He had eight sons. In Saul's time, Jesse was very old.
His three oldest sons had gone with Saul to the war. The firstborn was Eliab. The second was Abinadab. The third was Shammah.
David was the youngest. The three oldest had gone with Saul.
David went back and forth from Saul to take care of his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
The Philistine came near every morning and evening for forty days. He stood and shouted.
Jesse said to David, "Take a big bag of roasted grain and ten loaves of bread for your brothers. Carry them quickly to the camp.
Take ten cheeses to the army leader. See how your brothers are doing. Bring back news from them."
Saul and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah. They were fighting the Philistines.

David got up early in the morning. He left the sheep with a keeper. He took the food and went, just as Jesse had told him. He came to the camp as the army was going out to fight. They shouted the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines got their armies ready. They faced each other.
David left his things with the man who kept the things. He ran to the army lines. He said hello to his brothers.
While he was talking with them, the fighter Goliath came up from the Philistine lines. He said the same things again. David heard him.
All the men of Israel saw the man. They ran away from him. They were very afraid.

The men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man? He comes up to challenge Israel. The king will give a lot of money to the man who kills him. He will give his daughter to that man. He will also make that man's father's house free from taxes in Israel."

David asked the men standing near him, "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the shame from Israel? Who is this man who is not one of God's people? Why does he challenge the armies of the living God?"
The people answered him the same way. They said, "This is what will be done for the man who kills him."

Eliab, David's oldest brother, heard David talking to the men. Eliab was angry with David. He said, "Why did you come down here? With whom did you leave those few sheep in the desert? I know your pride and your mean heart. You came down just to see the battle."
David said, "What did I do now? I only asked a question."
He turned away from Eliab to another man. He asked the same thing. The people gave him the same answer.
