He said to his men, "The LORD would not want me to do this to my master. He is the one the LORD chose to be king. I will not hurt him."
David spoke firmly to his men. He did not let them hurt Saul. Then Saul left the cave and went on his way.
Then David came out of the cave. He called after Saul, "My lord the king!" Saul looked back. David bowed low with his face to the ground.
He said to Saul, "Why do you listen to people who say, 'David wants to hurt you'?

Today you saw with your own eyes how the LORD put you in my power in the cave. Some told me to kill you, but I did not. I said, 'I will not hurt my lord, because he is the one the LORD chose to be king.'

"Look, my father. Look at this piece of your robe in my hand. I cut off the corner of your robe, but I did not kill you. See that I have done nothing wrong. I have not hurt you. But you are chasing me to kill me.
"May the LORD judge between us. May the LORD pay you back for what you did to me, but I will not hurt you.
"People have an old saying: 'Bad people do bad things.' But I will not hurt you.
"Who is the king of Israel chasing? A dead dog? A flea?
"May the LORD be the judge between us. May He look at my side and stand up for me. May He save me from you."
When David finished, Saul said, "Is that your voice, David my son?" Then Saul cried loudly.
"You are more right than I am. You were good to me, but I was bad to you.
Today you told me the good you did for me. The LORD put me in your hands, but you did not kill me.
When a man finds his enemy, does he let him go safely? May the LORD pay you back with good for what you did for me today.
Now I know you will be king. The kingdom of Israel will be strong in your hands.
So swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my family after me. Do not wipe out my name from my father's family."
So David swore to Saul. Then Saul went home. David and his men went up to the safe place.
Samuel died. All Israel came together. They cried for him. They buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David got up and went down to the Desert of Paran.
A man in Maon had land in Carmel. He was very rich. He had 3,000 sheep and 1,000 goats. He was cutting the wool from his sheep in Carmel.
The man's name was Nabal. His wife's name was Abigail. She was smart and pretty. But the man was mean and did bad things.
David was in the desert. He heard that Nabal was cutting the wool from his sheep.
David sent ten young men. He said to them, "Go up to Nabal at Carmel. Greet him for me.
Say to him, 'Peace to you, your family, and all you have.'
I hear you have men cutting wool. Your shepherds were with us. We did not hurt them. We did not take anything from them the whole time they were in Carmel.
Ask your young men. They will tell you. Please let my men find favor with you, because we come on a good day. Give whatever you can to your servants and to your son David."
David's young men went and said all these things to Nabal in David's name. Then they waited.
Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is Jesse's son? There are many servants who run away from their masters these days.
Why should I take my bread, my water, and the meat I cooked for my wool cutters and give it to men I do not know where they come from?"
David's men turned around and went back. They told David everything Nabal said.

David said to his men, "Each of you strap on your sword." So each man strapped on his sword. David strapped on his sword too. About four hundred men went with David. Two hundred stayed with the supplies.
One of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "David sent messengers from the desert to greet our master. But he yelled at them.
Those men were very good to us. They did not shame us. They did not take anything from us the whole time we were with them in the fields.
They were like a wall around us, day and night, while we were with them watching the sheep.
Now think about what you will do. Trouble is coming to our master and all his family. He is such a bad man that no one can talk to him."
Abigail quickly took 200 loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five sheep that were ready, five baskets of roasted grain, 100 cakes of raisins, and 200 cakes of figs. She put them on donkeys.
She told her young men, "Go ahead of me. I will follow you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
She was riding on a donkey. She was going down the mountain in secret. David and his men were coming down to meet her. She met them.
David had said, "I guarded all this man had in the desert for nothing. Nothing of his was missing. But he paid me back with evil for good.
May God do the same to David's enemies, and more, if by morning I leave alive any male in his house."
When Abigail saw David, she quickly got off her donkey. She bowed with her face to the ground.
She fell at his feet and said, "My lord, let the blame be on me. Please let your servant speak to you. Listen to my words.
My lord, please do not pay attention to this bad man Nabal. His name means fool, and he acts like a fool. I am your servant. I did not see the young men you sent.

"Now, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as you live, the LORD has kept you from killing people and from saving yourself with your own hand. Now let your enemies and those who want to hurt you be like Nabal.
Please accept this gift that your servant has brought for you and your men.
Please forgive your servant's wrong. The LORD will surely make your family strong and lasting, because you fight the LORD's battles. No wrong will be found in you all your life.

If someone chases you to hurt you and take your life, your life will be kept safe with the LORD your God, like a treasure kept safe. But He will throw away your enemies' lives, like a stone thrown from a sling.

When The LORD does all the good He has promised about you, and makes you the leader of Israel, this will not trouble you. You will not be sorry that you spilled blood for no reason or paid back evil yourself.
When The LORD has been good to you, remember your servant."
David said to Abigail, "Praise the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today.
Praise your good sense. Praise you, because today you kept me from killing people and from paying back evil myself.
As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, He kept me from hurting you. If you had not come quickly to meet me, by morning not one male of Nabal's people would have been left alive."
David took from her hand what she had brought. He said to her, "Go home in peace. I have listened to you and accepted your request."
Abigail went to Nabal. He was in his house. He was having a feast like a king's feast. He was happy and very drunk. She did not tell him anything, big or small, until morning.
In the morning, when the wine was gone, Abigail told him everything. His heart died inside him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.

David heard that Nabal was dead. He said, "Praise the LORD, who stood up for me against the rude way Nabal treated me. He kept me from doing wrong. The LORD brought Nabal's wrong back on his own head." Then David sent word to Abigail to ask her to be his wife.
David's servants came to Abigail at Carmel. They said, "David sent us to you to take you as his wife."
She stood up and bowed with her face to the ground. She said, "Here I am, your servant. I am ready to wash the feet of my lord's servants."
Abigail quickly stood up and rode on a donkey. Five young women went with her. She followed David's messengers. She became his wife.
David had also married Ahinoam from Jezreel. Both of them became his wives.
But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
The men from Ziph came to Saul at Gibeah. They said, "David is hiding on the hill of Hakilah, near the desert."
So Saul took 3,000 chosen men from Israel. He went down to the desert of Ziph to look for David there.
Saul camped by the road on the hill of Hakilah, near the desert. David stayed in the desert. He saw that Saul had come after him.
David sent out spies. He learned that Saul had really come.
David went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw where Saul and Abner, son of Ner, the army leader, were lying. Saul lay inside the camp. The army camped around him.
David asked Ahimelek the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, "Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?" Abishai said, "I will go with you."
So David and Abishai went to the army at night. Saul was asleep inside the camp. His spear was stuck in the ground by his head. Abner and the soldiers lay around him.
Abishai said to David, "God has given your enemy to you today. Let me hit him once with the spear. I will not hit him twice."
But David said, "Do not kill him! Who can hurt the the LORD's chosen king and not be guilty?"
David also said, "I swear by the the LORD, the the LORD may strike him down. Or his time may come, and he may die. Or he may go to war and die."
But David said, "May the the LORD keep me from hurting the the LORD's chosen king. Now take the spear and the water jar by his head. Let's go."
David took the spear and the water jar from near Saul's head. They left. No one saw or knew. No one woke up. They were all asleep, because the the LORD had made them sleep deeply.
Then David crossed to the other side. He stood on top of a hill far away. There was a big space between them.
He called to the army and to Abner son of Ner. He said, "Abner, won't you answer me?" Abner answered, "Who is calling to the king?"
David said, "You are a man, aren't you? Who is like you in Israel? Why did you not guard your lord the king? Someone came to kill your lord the king.

What you did is not good. I swear by the the LORD, you and your men should die, because you did not guard your master, the the LORD's chosen king. Look around. Where are the king's spear and water jar that were by his head?"
Saul knew David's voice. He said, "Is that your voice, David my son?" David said, "Yes, my lord the king.
Why does my lord chase his servant? What have I done? What wrong did I do?

Now, my lord the king, please listen to me. If the the LORD made you turn against me, may He accept a gift. But if people did it, may they be cursed before the the LORD. They drove me out today from sharing in the the LORD's land. They said, 'Go serve other gods.'
Now do not let my blood fall to the ground away from the the LORD. The king of Israel came out to look for a flea, like someone hunting a bird in the mountains."
Saul said, "I have sinned. Come back, David my son. Because you treated my life as precious today, I will not harm you again. I have acted like a fool. I was very wrong."
David said, "Here is the king's spear. Let one of your young men come over and get it.
The LORD gives each man what he deserves for doing right and being faithful. The LORD gave you to me today, but I would not hurt the the LORD's chosen king.
As your life was precious to me today, may my life be precious to the the LORD. May He save me from all trouble."
Saul said to David, "You are blessed, David my son. You will do great things and win." Then David went on his way, and Saul went home.
David said to himself, "One day Saul will catch me. It is best for me to run to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will stop looking for me all over Israel, and I will get away from him."
So David and his six hundred men went to Achish son of Maoc, king of Gath.
David and his men lived in Gath with Achish. Each man brought his family. David had two wives: Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail from Carmel, who had been Nabal's wife.
When Saul heard that David had run to Gath, he stopped looking for him.
David said to Achish, "If you are happy with me, give me a place in one of the far towns, so I can live there. Why should your servant live with you in your city?"
So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. Even now it belongs to the kings of Judah.
David lived in the land of the Philistines for one year and four months.
David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites. These people had lived in that land for a long time, from Shur all the way to Egypt.
When David attacked the land, he did not leave a man or woman alive. He took sheep, cows, donkeys, camels, and clothes. Then he went back to Achish.
Achish would ask, "Where did you raid today?" David would answer, "In the south of Judah," or "In the south of the Jerahmeelites," or "In the south of the Kenites."
David did not let anyone live to be taken to Gath. He said, "They might tell on us and say, 'Look what David did.'" He did this the whole time he lived in the land of the Philistines.
Achish trusted David. He thought, "David has made his own people hate him. So he will be my servant forever."
At that time, the Philistines gathered their armies to fight Israel. Achish said to David, "You know for sure that you and your men will go out with me in the camp."
David said to Achish, "Then you will know what your servant can do." Achish said to David, "Then I will make you my bodyguard forever."
Samuel had died. All Israel was sad and buried him in Ramah, his town. Saul had sent away all the people who talk to spirits.
The Philistines came and camped at Shunem. Saul gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa.
Saul saw the Philistine camp. He was afraid, and his heart shook very much.
Saul asked the the LORD for help, but the the LORD did not answer him. He did not answer by dreams, by the Urim stones, or by prophets.
Saul said to his servants, "Find me a woman who talks to spirits. I will go to her and ask her for help." His servants said, "There is a woman who talks to spirits at En Dor."
Saul put on other clothes to hide who he was. He and two men went to the woman at night. He said, "Please tell my future by a spirit. Bring up for me the person I name."
The woman said, "You know what Saul did. He took the people who talk to spirits out of the land. Why are you trying to trap me and kill me?"
Saul promised her by the the LORD, "As the the LORD lives, no harm will come to you for this."
The woman said, "Who should I bring up for you?" Saul said, "Bring up Samuel for me."
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out loudly. The woman said to Saul, "Why did you trick me? You are Saul!"
The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" The woman said to Saul, "I see a spirit coming up from the ground."
Saul said, "What does he look like?" The woman said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wearing a robe." Saul knew it was Samuel. He bowed his face to the ground.

Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you bothered me by bringing me up?" Saul said, "I am in great trouble. The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has left me. He does not answer me anymore, not by prophets or by dreams. So I called you to tell me what to do."
Samuel said, "Why do you ask me? The the LORD has left you and become your enemy."
Samuel said, "The The LORD has done what He said through me. The The LORD has torn the kingdom from your hand and given it to your neighbor David."
Samuel said, "Because you did not obey the the LORD and did not carry out His fierce anger against Amalek, the the LORD has done this to you today."

Samuel said, "The The LORD will also give Israel with you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The The LORD will also give the army of Israel into the hands of the Philistines."
Saul quickly fell full length on the ground. He was very afraid of Samuel's words. He had no strength, because he had not eaten all day or all night.
The woman came to Saul. She saw that he was very upset. She said, "Look, your servant listened to you. I risked my life and did what you said.
Now please listen to me too. Let me put a piece of bread in front of you. Eat, so you will have strength for your trip."
He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants and the woman urged him. He listened to them. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fat calf in the house. She hurried and killed it. She took flour, kneaded it, and baked bread without yeast.
She set the food in front of Saul and his servants. They ate. Then they got up and left that night.
The Philistines brought all their armies to Aphek. The people of Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel.
The Philistine leaders marched by hundreds and by thousands. David and his men marched last with Achish.

The Philistine leaders said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish said to the Philistine leaders, "This is David. He served Saul, the king of Israel. He has been with me for days or years. I have not found anything wrong with him since the day he came to me."

The Philistine leaders were angry with Achish. They said, "Send the man back. Let him go to the place you gave him. He must not go with us to battle. He might turn against us in the fight. He could win back his master's favor by killing our men."
"Isn't this David? The people sang about him in dances. They said, 'Saul killed thousands, but David killed tens of thousands.'"

Achish called David and said to him, "I swear by the LORD that you have been good and right in my eyes. I would be glad for you to go out and come in with me in the army. I have found no wrong in you from the day you came to me until now. But the leaders do not approve of you.
Now go back. Go in peace. Do not make the Philistine leaders angry."
David said to Achish, "What have I done? What wrong have you found in your servant since I came before you until today? Why can't I go and fight the enemies of my king?"
Achish answered David, "I know you are good in my eyes, like an angel of God. But the Philistine leaders said, 'He must not go up with us to battle.'
So get up early in the morning. You and your master's servants who came with you should leave when it is light."
David and his men got up early. They went back to the land of the Philistines. The Philistines went up to Jezreel.
On the third day, David and his men came to Ziklag. The Amalekites had attacked the south country and Ziklag. They attacked Ziklag and burned it down.
They took the women and everyone else there, young and old. They did not kill anyone. They just led them away.
When David and his men came to the city, they saw it burned down. Their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken away.
David and the people with him cried out loud. They cried until they had no strength left to cry.
David's two wives were taken too. One was Ahinoam from Jezreel. The other was Abigail, who had been Nabal's wife from Carmel.
David was very upset. The people wanted to throw stones at him. They were all very sad because of their sons and daughters. But David found new strength in the LORD his God.
Then David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Please bring me the special vest." So Abiathar brought it to David.
David asked the LORD, "Should I chase these attackers? Will I catch them?" The LORD said, "Chase them. You will catch them and save the captives."
So David and his six hundred men went. They came to the Brook Besor. Some men stayed there.
David and four hundred men kept chasing. Two hundred men were too tired to cross the brook, so they stayed behind.
David's men found an Egyptian man in a field. They brought him to David. They gave him water to drink and food to eat.
They gave him a piece of fig cake and two bunches of raisins. He ate and felt better. He had not eaten or drunk for three days and three nights.
David asked him, "Who do you belong to? Where are you from?" The man said, "I am an Egyptian. I am a slave of an Amalekite. My master left me three days ago because I was sick.
We attacked the south country of the Cherethites, the land of Judah, and the south country of Caleb. We also burned Ziklag."
David asked him, "Can you lead me to these attackers?" He said, "Promise me by God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master. Then I will lead you to them."

So he led David there. The attackers were spread out over the whole area. They were eating, drinking, and having a party. They had taken many things from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah.
David fought them from evening until the next evening. No one got away except four hundred young men on camels.
David got back everything the Amalekites had taken. He also got back his two wives.
Nothing was missing. Not one small thing or big thing, not sons or daughters, not any of the things they had taken. David brought it all back.
David took all the sheep and cattle. His men drove them ahead of the rest of the animals and said, "This is David's share of what he took."
David came to the two hundred men who had been too tired to follow him. They had stayed at the Brook Besor. They came out to meet David and the people with him. David greeted them.
But some bad and useless men who had gone with David said, "They did not go with us, so we should not give them any of the things we took. They can take their wives and children and go."
But David said, "No, my brothers. We must not do that with what the LORD has given us. He kept us safe and let us beat the attackers who came against us.
Who would agree with you about this? The man who goes to fight gets the same share as the man who stays with the supplies. They will share the same."
From that day on, David made this a rule for Israel.
When David got back to Ziklag, he sent some of the things he had taken to his friends, the elders of Judah. He said, "Here is a gift for you from the things taken from the LORD's enemies."
He sent gifts to the people in Bethel, in Ramoth in the south country, and in Jattir.
He sent gifts to the people in Aroer, in Siphmoth, and in Eshtemoa.
He sent gifts to the people in Racal, in the towns of the Jerahmeelites, and in the towns of the Kenites.
He sent gifts to the people in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, and in Athach.
He sent gifts to the people in Hebron and to all the places where David and his men had gone.
The Philistines fought against Israel. The Israelites ran away from them. Many Israelites died on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines chased Saul and his sons. They killed his sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua.
The fight was hard around Saul. Men with bows caught up to him and shot him. He was hurt very badly.

Saul said to the man who carried his weapons, "Draw your sword and kill me with it. If not, these men who are not God's people will come and kill me and hurt me." But the man was very afraid. He would not do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it.
The man who carried his weapons saw that Saul was dead. He fell on his own sword too. He died with Saul.
So Saul, his three sons, his helper, and all the men with him died on that same day.

The Israelites across the valley and across the Jordan saw that their army had run away. They saw that Saul and his sons were dead. So they left their towns and ran away too. The Philistines moved in and lived there.
The next day the Philistines came to take things from the dead. They found Saul and his three sons on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head. They took off his armor. They sent men all around the land of the Philistines to tell the news in the temples of their gods and to the people.
They put his armor in the temple of Ashtoreth. They hung his body on the wall of Beth Shan.
The people of Jabesh Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul.
All their brave men walked all night. They took the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth Shan. They brought them to Jabesh. They burned them there.
Then they took the bones and buried them under a tree in Jabesh. They did not eat for seven days.
After Saul died, David came back from fighting the Amalekites. He stayed in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from Saul's camp. His clothes were torn, and dirt was on his head. He came to David, fell to the ground, and bowed down.
David asked him, "Where did you come from?" The man said, "I ran away from Israel's camp."
David said, "What happened? Tell me." The man said, "Our people ran from the battle. Many died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too."
David asked the young man, "How do you know Saul and Jonathan are dead?"
"I happened to be on Mount Gilboa. Saul was leaning on his spear. The chariots and horsemen were close to him.
He turned and saw me. He called to me. I said, 'Here I am.'
He asked, 'Who are you?' I said, 'I am an Amalekite.'
"He said, 'Stand over me and kill me. I am in great pain, but I am still alive.'
So I stood over him and killed him. I knew he could not live after he fell. I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm. I brought them to you, my lord."
David grabbed his clothes and tore them. All the men with him did the same.
They cried and did not eat until evening. They were sad for Saul, Jonathan, the the LORD's people, and Israel. They died by the sword.
David asked the young man, "Where are you from?" He said, "I am an Amalekite. My father was a foreigner."
David said, "Why were you not afraid to hurt the the LORD's chosen king?"
David called one of the young men and said, "Go and strike him." The young man struck him, and he died.
David said, "Your blood is on your own head. Your mouth spoke against you. You said, 'I killed the the LORD's chosen king.'"
David sang a sad song for Saul and Jonathan.
David said, "Teach the people of Judah the bow song. It is written in the Book of Jashar."
"Israel, your pride lies dead on your hills. How the mighty have fallen!
Do not tell this in Gath. Do not say it in the streets of Ashkelon. The Philistine girls might be glad. Girls from other lands might cheer.
Mountains of Gilboa, may no dew or rain fall on you. May your fields not grow grain. For there the shield of the mighty was thrown down. Saul's shield was left without oil."
"From the blood of the dead and the fat of the mighty, Jonathan's bow did not turn back. Saul's sword did not come back empty.
Saul and Jonathan were loved and pleasant in life. In death they were not parted. They were faster than eagles. They were stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, cry for Saul. He clothed you in red with nice things. He put gold jewelry on your clothes."
"How the mighty have fallen in battle! Jonathan is dead on your hills.
I am sad for you, Jonathan my brother. You were very kind to me. Your love for me was wonderful. It was more than the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen! The weapons of war are gone."
After that, David asked the LORD, "Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah?" The LORD said, "Go up." David asked, "Where should I go up?" The LORD said, "To Hebron."
David went up with his two wives. One was Ahinoam from Jezreel. The other was Abigail, who had been Nabal's wife from Carmel.
David also brought the men who were with him. Each man brought his family. They lived in the towns near Hebron.
The men of Judah came to David. They made him king over the people of Judah. They told David, "The men of Jabesh-gilead buried Saul."
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead. He said, "May you be blessed by the LORD. You were kind to Saul, your lord. You buried him.
"Now may the LORD be kind and faithful to you. I will do the same good thing for you, because you did this for Saul.
"Now let your hands be strong. Be brave men. Your lord Saul is dead. The people of Judah have made me king over them."
But Abner, the son of Ner, was the leader of Saul's army. He took Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, and brought him to Mahanaim.
Abner made Ish-bosheth king over Gilead, Ashur, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he became king over Israel. He ruled for two years. But the people of Judah followed David.
David was king in Hebron over the people of Judah for seven years and six months.
Abner and the servants of Ish-bosheth went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab, the son of Zeruiah, and David's servants went out too. They met by the pool of Gibeon. One group sat on one side of the pool, and the other group sat on the other side.
Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men get up and fight before us." Joab said, "Let them get up."
So twelve men from Benjamin and Ish-bosheth stood up, and twelve of David's men.
Each man grabbed the man across from him by the head and stabbed him in the side. They all fell down together. That place in Gibeon was called Helkath-hazzurim.
The battle was very hard that day. Abner and the men of Israel lost to David's men.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel could run as fast as a deer in a field.
Asahel chased Abner. He did not turn to the right or to the left.
Abner looked behind him and said, "Is that you, Asahel?" Asahel said, "Yes, it is me."
Abner said, "Turn to your right or your left. Grab one of the young men and take his armor for yourself." But Asahel would not stop chasing him.
Abner said again, "Stop chasing me. Why should I hit you and knock you to the ground? How could I face your brother Joab?"

But Asahel would not turn. So Abner stabbed him in the stomach with the back end of his spear. The spear came out his back. Asahel fell and died there. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel fell and died stopped.
Joab and Abishai chased Abner. The sun was going down when they reached the hill of Ammah near Giah, on the way to the desert of Gibeon.
The men of Benjamin gathered behind Abner. They stood together on top of a hill.
Abner called to Joab, "Must the sword kill forever? Don't you know this will end in sorrow? How long before you tell the people to stop chasing their brothers?"
Joab said, "As surely as God lives, if you had not spoken, the people would have chased their brothers until morning."
Joab blew the trumpet. All the people stopped. They did not chase Israel anymore, and they did not fight anymore.
Abner and his men walked all night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan River and went to Mahanaim.
Joab came back from chasing Abner. He gathered all the people. David's men were missing nineteen men and Asahel.
But David's men had killed 360 men from Benjamin and Abner's men.
They carried Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Joab and his men walked all night and reached Hebron at sunrise.
The war between Saul's family and David's family lasted a long time. David got stronger and stronger, but Saul's family got weaker and weaker.
David had sons in Hebron. His first son was Amnon. His mother was Ahinoam from Jezreel.
His second son was Chileab. His mother was Abigail, who had been Nabal's wife from Carmel. His third son was Absalom. His mother was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.
His fourth son was Adonijah. His mother was Haggith. His fifth son was Shephatiah. His mother was Abital.
His sixth son was Ithream. His mother was David's wife Eglah. These sons were born to David in Hebron.
While the war went on between Saul's family and David's family, Abner became strong in Saul's family.
Saul had a woman named Rizpah. She was Aiah's daughter. Ish-Bosheth said to Abner, "Why did you sleep with my father's woman?"

Abner was very angry about what Ish-Bosheth said. He said, "Do you think I am a nobody from Judah? Today I am kind to your father Saul's family, his brothers, and his friends. I have not handed you over to David. But today you blame me for something about this woman."
"May God punish me if I do not do for David what the the LORD promised him.
I will help move the kingdom from Saul's family and make David king over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."
Ish-Bosheth was afraid of Abner, so he could not answer him.
Abner sent messengers to David. They said, "Whose land is this? Make a covenant with me, and I will help you bring all Israel to you."
David said, "Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing. You will not see my face unless you bring my wife Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see me."
David sent messengers to Ish-Bosheth, Saul's son. They said, "Give me my wife Michal. I paid for her with one hundred Philistine foreskins."
Ish-Bosheth sent men and took Michal from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband walked with her and cried as he went. He followed her to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go back." So he went back.
Abner talked with the elders of Israel. He said, "In the past you wanted David to be your king. Now do what you need to do.
The The LORD has spoken about David. He said, 'By the hand of My servant David, I will save My people Israel from the Philistines and all their enemies.'"
Abner also spoke to the people of Benjamin. Then he went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and Benjamin's family thought was good.
Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men. David made a feast for Abner and his men.

Abner said to David, "Let me go and gather all Israel for my lord the king. Then they can make a covenant with you, and you can rule over all that your heart wants." David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
Just then, David's servants and Joab came back from a raid. They brought much treasure. Abner was not with David in Hebron anymore, because David had sent him away in peace.
Joab and all his men came in. They told Joab, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king sent him away in peace."
Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why did you send him away? Now he is gone!"
You know Abner son of Ner. He came to trick you and learn where you go and what you do."
Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well of Sirah. David did not know about this.
When Abner came back to Hebron, Joab took him aside at the gate to speak quietly. There Joab stabbed him in the stomach, and Abner died.
When David heard about it, he said, "I and my kingdom are not guilty before the the LORD for the blood of Abner son of Ner."

He said, "May this trouble fall on Joab and his father's family. May Joab's family never be without someone who is sick, or has a skin disease, or leans on a staff, or dies by the sword, or has no bread."
Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner. They did this because Abner had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and all the people with him, "Tear your clothes. Put on sackcloth. Mourn for Abner." King David followed the coffin.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king cried loudly at Abner's grave. All the people cried too.
The king sang a sad song for Abner. He said, "Should Abner die like a fool?"
"Your hands were not tied. Your feet were not chained. You fell like a man killed by bad men." All the people cried again over him.
All the people came to David to eat bread while it was still day. But David made a strong promise. He said, "May God punish me if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down."
All the people noticed this, and it pleased them. Everything the king did was good in the people's eyes.
All Israel and all the people knew that day that the king had not wanted Abner son of Ner to die.
The king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a great leader and prince died today in Israel?"
"I am weak today, even though I am the chosen king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too strong for me. May the the LORD pay back the one who does evil with the evil he has done."
When Saul's son heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost courage. All of Israel was afraid.

Saul's son had two men who were leaders of soldiers. One was named Baanah, and the other was named Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, and they were from the family of Benjamin. Beeroth was counted as part of Benjamin.
The people of Beeroth ran away to Gittaim. They lived there as strangers until this day.

Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son who could not walk well. He was five years old when news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and ran. As she hurried, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, went to Ish-bosheth's house. It was the hot part of the day, at noon. Ish-bosheth was lying on his bed.
They went into the middle of the house as if to get some wheat. Then they stabbed him in the stomach. Rechab and his brother Baanah got away.

They went into the house while he was lying on his bed in his bedroom. They struck him and killed him. Then they cut off his head and took it with them. They traveled all night along the road through the Arabah.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. They said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy. He tried to kill you. Today the the LORD has paid back Saul and his family for what they did to you."
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth. He said, "As surely as the the LORD lives, who saved me from all trouble,
when someone told me, 'Saul is dead,' thinking he was bringing good news, I grabbed him and killed him at Ziklag. That was his reward for bringing that news.
How much more should I now make you pay for killing a good man in his own house while he lay on his bed? I will remove you from the earth."

David gave an order to his young men. They killed Rechab and Baanah. They cut off their hands and feet. Then they hung them by the pool in Hebron. They also took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in Abner's grave in Hebron.
All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron. They said, "We are your own family.
In the past, when Saul was king, you led Israel out and brought them back. The LORD said to you, 'You will take care of My people Israel. You will be their leader.'"
All the leaders of Israel came to King David at Hebron. They made an agreement with him before the LORD. They poured oil on David and made him king over Israel.
David was 30 years old when he became king. He ruled for 40 years.
He ruled Judah from Hebron for 7 and a half years. Then he ruled all Israel and Judah from Jerusalem for 33 years.

The king and his men went to Jerusalem to fight the Jebusites who lived there. The Jebusites said to David, "You cannot come in here. Even blind and lame people can stop you." They thought David would never get in.
But David captured the fort of Zion. It became the City of David.

That day David said, "Whoever attacks the Jebusites must go up the water tunnel. He must reach the blind and lame people David hates." So people say, "Blind and lame people cannot come into the house."
David lived in the fort. He called it the City of David. He built all around it, from the wall inward.
David became stronger and stronger. The LORD God of All Armies was with him.
Hiram, king of Tyre, sent men to David. They brought cedar wood, wood workers, and stone workers. They built a house for David.
David knew the LORD had made him king over Israel. He knew the LORD had made his kingdom strong for His people Israel.
After David came from Hebron, he took more wives and servant wives in Jerusalem. More sons and daughters were born to him.
Their names were Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon.
Then came Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, and Japhia.
Then came Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
The Philistines heard David had been made king over Israel. They came to look for him. David heard about it and went down to his fort.
The Philistines came and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
David asked the LORD, "Should I go and fight the Philistines? Will You give them to me?" The LORD said, "Go. I will give the Philistines to you."
David went to Baal-perazim and beat them there. He said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies in front of me like a flood of water." So he named that place Baal-perazim.
The Philistines left their false gods there. David and his men carried them away.
The Philistines came again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
David asked the LORD what to do.

The LORD said, "Do not go straight up. Go around behind them. Come at them from in front of the trees. When you hear a sound like marching on top of the trees, hurry. Then I will go out ahead of you to strike the Philistine camp."
David did what the LORD told him. He struck the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
David brought together the best men of Israel again. There were thirty thousand of them.
David and all the people with him left Baale of Judah. They went to bring the ark of God from there. The ark is called by the Name—the name of the the LORD of Hosts. He sits between the cherubim.
They put the ark of God on a new cart. They brought it from Abinadab's house on the hill. Abinadab's sons, Uzzah and Ahio, were leading the new cart.
They brought the ark of God with it. Ahio walked in front of the ark.
David and all the people of Israel celebrated before the the LORD. They played wooden instruments, harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, rattles, and cymbals.
When they came to Nacon's grain floor, the oxen stumbled. Uzzah reached out and held the ark of God.
The The LORD was very angry with Uzzah. God struck him down there because he did not show respect. He died there beside the ark of God.
David was angry because the the LORD had struck Uzzah. He named that place Perez-uzzah. People still call it that today.
That day David was afraid of the the LORD. He said, "How can the ark of the the LORD come to me?"
So David did not want to take the ark of the the LORD to the City of David. He took it to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of the the LORD stayed in Obed-edom's house for three months. The The LORD blessed Obed-edom and his whole family.

Someone told King David, "The The LORD has blessed Obed-edom's house and all he owns, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought the ark of God from Obed-edom's house to the City of David with joy.
When the men carrying the ark of the the LORD had taken six steps, David sacrificed an ox and a fat calf.
David wore a linen vest. He danced with all his strength before the the LORD.
So David and all the people of Israel brought up the ark of the the LORD. They shouted and blew trumpets.

As the ark of the the LORD came into the City of David, Saul's daughter Michal looked through a window. She saw King David jumping and dancing before the the LORD. She looked down on him in her heart.
They brought the ark of the the LORD and put it in its place. It was inside the tent David had set up for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the the LORD.
When David finished offering the burnt and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the the LORD of Hosts.
Then he gave every man and woman in Israel's crowd a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. Then all the people went home.

As David came home to bless his family, Saul's daughter Michal came out to meet him. She said, "How great the king of Israel looked today! He showed himself to the servant girls, like a foolish man would."

But David said to Michal, "I was dancing before the the LORD. He chose me over your father and all his family. He made me ruler over the the LORD's people Israel. I will celebrate before the the LORD,
I will make myself even lower than this. I will think even less of myself. But those servant girls you talked about will honor me."
Michal, Saul's daughter, had no children until the day she died.
When King David was living in his house, the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies around him.
The king said to Nathan the prophet, "Look, I live in a house made of cedar wood. But the ark of God stays in a tent."
Nathan said to the king, "Do everything you want. the LORD is with you."
But that night, the word of the LORD came to Nathan. He said,
"Go and tell My servant David: This is what the LORD says: Will you build a house for Me to live in?
I have not lived in a house since the day I brought the people of Israel out of Egypt. I have moved about in a tent.
Everywhere I walked with all the people of Israel, I never asked any tribe I told to take care of My people Israel why they had not built Me a house of cedar."
"Now say this to My servant David: This is what the LORD of Armies says: I took you from the sheep pen, from following the sheep, to be ruler over My people Israel.
I was with you everywhere you went. I cut off all your enemies before you. I will make your name great, like the names of the great people on earth.
I will give a place to My people Israel. I will plant them there. They will live there and not be moved anymore. Wicked people will not hurt them again, like before.
From the day I put judges over My people Israel, I have given you rest from all your enemies. The LORD tells you that the LORD will make a house for you."
"When your days are full and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your child after you, who comes from your body. I will make his kingdom strong.
He will build a house for My name. I will set up his kingdom forever.
I will be his Father, and he will be My Son. If he sins, I will correct him with a stick and with blows from people.
But My faithful love will not leave him, like I took it from Saul, whom I took from before you.
Your house and your kingdom will last forever before you. Your throne will be set up forever."
Nathan told David all these words and all this vision.
Then King David went in and sat before the LORD. He said,
"Who am I, Lord, the LORD, and what is my family, that You brought me this far?
This is still small in Your eyes, Lord, the LORD. You have spoken about Your servant's house for a long time. Is this how You usually treat people, Lord, the LORD?
You did this because of Your word and because of Your heart. You have shown Your servant this great thing."
"So You are great, Lord, the LORD. There is no one like You. There is no God besides You, from all we have heard.

Who is like Your people Israel? They are one nation on earth that God went to save for Himself. He did this to make a name for Himself. He did great and scary things for Your land, driving out nations and their gods before Your people, whom You saved from Egypt.
You made Your people Israel Your people forever. You, the LORD, became their God."
"Now, the LORD God, keep forever the word You spoke about Your servant and his house. Do what You said.
Let Your name be great forever. Then people will say that the LORD of Armies is God over Israel. The house of Your servant David will be set up before You.
You, the LORD of Armies, God of Israel, have told Your servant that You will build him a house. So Your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to You.
Now, Lord, the LORD, You are God. Your words are true. You have promised this good thing to Your servant.
Now please bless Your servant's house. Let it last forever before You. Lord, the LORD, You have spoken. Your servant's house will be blessed forever by Your blessing."
After this, David defeated the Philistines and brought them under his rule. He took Metheg Ammah from them.
He defeated Moab too. He made them lie on the ground and measured them with a rope. He killed two out of three and let one out of three live. Moab became David's servants and brought gifts.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when Hadadezer went to take back his power by the Euphrates River.
David captured 1,700 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers from him. He crippled all the chariot horses, but he kept 100 chariots.
When the Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David killed 22,000 of them.
David placed soldiers in Damascus of Aram. The Arameans became David's servants and brought gifts. The LORD gave David victory everywhere he went.
David took the gold shields that belonged to Hadadezer's officers and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, David took a lot of bronze.
When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated all of Hadadezer's army,

he sent his son Joram to King David. Joram came to greet David and wish him well, because David had fought and defeated Hadadezer. Hadadezer had been at war with Toi. Joram brought gifts of silver, gold, and bronze.
King David set these gifts apart for the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had set apart from all the nations he conquered.
He set apart gifts from Aram, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the things taken from Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David became famous when he came back from killing 18,000 Arameans in the Valley of Salt.
He placed soldiers all through Edom. All of Edom became David's servants. The LORD gave David victory everywhere he went.
David ruled over all Israel. He did what was fair and right for all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the records.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests. Seraiah was the secretary.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites. David's sons were priests.
David asked, "Is there anyone still left from Saul's family? I want to show kindness to them because of Jonathan."
They called Ziba, a servant from Saul's house, to come to David. The king asked him, "Are you Ziba?" He answered, "Yes, I am your servant."
The king said, "Is there anyone left in Saul's family? I want to show God's kindness to him." Ziba said, "Yes, Jonathan has a son. Both his feet are hurt, so he cannot walk."
The king asked, "Where is he?" Ziba said, "He is at the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo-debar."
King David sent men and brought him from there.
Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, came to David. He bowed down with his face to the ground. David said, "Mephibosheth!" He answered, "Here I am, your servant."
David said, "Do not be afraid. I will show you kindness because of your father Jonathan. I will give you back all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul. You will always eat at my table."
Mephibosheth bowed down and said, "Who am I, your servant, that you would care about a nobody like me?"
Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "I have given your master's son everything that belonged to Saul and his family.

You, your sons, and your servants must work the land for him. Bring in the crops so your master's grandson has food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master's grandson, will always eat at my table." Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, "Your servant will do everything my lord the king tells him to do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. All who lived in Ziba's house became servants to Mephibosheth.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table. He could not walk because both his feet were hurt.
After this, the king of the Ammonites died. His son Hanun became king.
David said, "I will be kind to Hanun son of Nahash, just like his father was kind to me." So David sent men to comfort him. They went to the land of Ammon.

The leaders of the Ammonites said to Hanun, their lord, "Do you think David is honoring your father? He sent men to comfort you. But David may have sent them to look around the city, spy on it, and destroy it."
So Hanun took David's men. He shaved off half of each man's beard. He cut their clothes in half up to their hips. Then he sent them away.
People told David what happened. He sent men to meet them, because they were very ashamed. The king said, "Stay in Jericho until your beards grow back. Then come home."
The Ammonites saw that David was angry with them. So they hired soldiers from Aram. They got 20,000 foot soldiers from Beth Rehob and Zobah, 12,000 men from Maacah, and men from Tob.
David heard about it. He sent Joab and all his strong soldiers.
The Ammonites came out and got ready to fight at the city gate. The Arameans from Zobah, Rehob, Tob, and Maacah stayed out in the field by themselves.
Joab saw that the enemy was in front of him and behind him. He picked the best soldiers of Israel and lined them up against the Arameans.
He gave the rest of the men to his brother Abishai. They lined up against the Ammonites.
Joab said, "If the Arameans are too strong for me, you come help me. If the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come save you."
He also said, "Be strong! Let us be brave for our people and for the cities of our God. And may the LORD do what is good in His eyes."
Joab and his men moved forward to fight the Arameans. The Arameans ran away.
When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had run away, they also ran from Abishai. They went back into the city. Then Joab left the Ammonites and went back to Jerusalem.
The Arameans saw that Israel had beaten them. So they came together again.
Hadadezer sent for more Arameans from across the river. They came to Helam. Shobach, the leader of Hadadezer's army, led them.
Someone told David. He gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan River, and went to Helam. The Arameans lined up against David and fought him.
The Arameans ran from Israel. David killed 700 chariot soldiers and 40,000 horse soldiers. He also hit Shobach, the army leader, and Shobach died there.
All the kings who served Hadadezer saw that Israel had beaten them. They made peace with Israel and served Israel. The Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites again.
In the spring, when kings go to war, David sent Joab with his officers and all of Israel's army. They defeated the Ammonites and surrounded Rabbah. But David stayed in Jerusalem.
One evening David got up from his bed and walked on the roof of the king's house. From the roof he saw a woman washing. She was very beautiful.
David sent someone to ask about her. The man said, "She is Bathsheba. She is the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite."
David sent messengers to bring her. She came to him, and he slept with her. She had just finished her monthly washing. Then she went home.
The woman became pregnant. She sent word to David and said, "I am pregnant."
Then David sent word to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah came, David asked him how Joab was, how the men were, and how the war was going.
David said to Uriah, "Go home and rest." Uriah left the king's house. A gift from the king was sent after him.
But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all his master's servants. He did not go home.
David was told that Uriah did not go home. So David asked Uriah, "You just came from a trip. Why didn't you go home?"

Uriah said to David, "The ark of God and the people of Israel and Judah are staying in tents. My lord Joab and his men are camped in the fields. How could I go home to eat and drink and lie with my wife? I promise I will not do that!"
David said to him, "Stay here one more day. Tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him to eat and drink. David made him drunk. That evening Uriah went out to sleep on his mat with his master's servants. He did not go home.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, "Put Uriah in the front where the fight is hardest. Then pull back from him so he will be hit and die."
While Joab was attacking the city, he put Uriah where he knew the strongest enemy soldiers were.
The men of the city came out and fought Joab. Some of David's men died. Uriah the Hittite died too.
Joab sent David a full report about the battle.
He told the messenger, "When you finish telling the king about the battle,
the king may get angry. He may ask, 'Why did you go so close to the city to fight? Didn't you know they shoot arrows from the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerub-Besheth? Didn't a woman throw a heavy stone on him from the wall, so he died in Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' Then tell him, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.'"
The messenger went and told David everything Joab had sent him to say.
The messenger said to David, "The men were stronger than us. They came out against us in the open field. But we pushed them back to the city gate.
Then the archers shot down at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's men died. Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too."
David said to the messenger, "Tell Joab, 'Do not worry about this. War kills one man as well as another. Fight harder against the city and destroy it.' Tell him this to cheer him up."
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him.
After her time of sadness was over, David brought her to his house. She became his wife and had a son. But what David had done did not please the LORD.
The LORD sent Nathan to David. Nathan went to him and said, "There were two men in one city. One was rich, and one was poor.
The rich man had many sheep and cows.

The poor man had nothing but one little lamb. He bought it and raised it. It grew up with him and his children. It ate his food, drank from his cup, and slept in his arms. It was like a daughter to him.
A traveler came to the rich man. The rich man did not want to take one of his own sheep or cows for the guest. He took the poor man's lamb and cooked it for the man who came to him."
David was very angry with that man. He said to Nathan, "I swear by the LORD, the man who did this should die!
He must pay back the lamb four times, because he did this and had no pity."
Nathan said to David, "You are that man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I chose you to be king over Israel. I saved you from Saul.
I gave you your master's house and his wives. I gave you the people of Israel and Judah. If that was not enough, I would have given you even more.

"Why did you turn away from the LORD's word and do what is bad in His eyes? You killed Uriah the Hittite with a sword. You took his wife to be your wife. You had the Ammonites kill him with their swords.
So now war will never leave your family. You turned away from Me, and you took Uriah's wife to be your wife.

"This is what the LORD says: 'Look, I will bring trouble on you from your own family. I will take your wives while you watch. I will give them to your neighbor. He will sleep with your wives in the sunlight.
You did your wrong in secret. But I will do this where all Israel can see it, in the sunlight.'"
David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan said to David, "The LORD has taken away your sin. You will not die.
But because you made the LORD look bad by this thing, the baby born to you will die."
Then Nathan went home. The LORD struck the baby that Uriah's wife had for David, and the baby became sick.
David prayed to God for the baby. He did not eat. He went in and lay on the ground all night.
The older men of his house stood over him to help him up, but he would not get up. He did not eat with them.

On the seventh day the baby died. David's servants were afraid to tell him. They said, "While the baby was alive, we talked to him, but he would not listen. How can we tell him the baby is dead? He might hurt himself."
David saw his servants whispering. He knew the baby was dead. He said to them, "Is the baby dead?" They said, "He is dead."
David got up from the ground. He washed, put on oil, and changed his clothes. He went to the LORD's house and worshiped. Then he went home. He asked for food, and they gave him bread, and he ate.
His servants said to him, "Why did you do this? You did not eat and you cried while the baby was alive. But when the baby died, you got up and ate."
He said, "While the baby was alive, I did not eat and I cried. I thought, 'Who knows? The LORD may be kind to me, and the baby may live.'
But now he is dead. Why should I keep fasting? Can I bring him back? I will go to him, but he will not come back to me."
David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He went to her and slept with her. She had a son. He named him Solomon. The LORD loved him.
The LORD sent a message through Nathan the prophet to name the baby Jedidiah, because the LORD loved him.
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites. He captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David. He said, "I have fought against Rabbah. I have also captured the city by the water.
Now bring the rest of the people. Camp around the city and capture it. If I capture it, it may be named after me."
David gathered all the people. He went to Rabbah. He fought against it and captured it.
He took the crown from their king's head. It was gold and very heavy. It had an expensive stone. They put it on David's head. He also took many valuable things from the city.

He brought out the people who were there. He made them work with saws, iron picks, and iron axes. He made them work at the brick ovens. David did this to all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all the people went back to Jerusalem.
After this, David's son Absalom had a beautiful sister named Tamar. David's son Amnon loved her.
Amnon was so upset about Tamar that he felt sick. She was not married yet, and he thought he could not be with her.

But the people said, "No, you should not go. If we run away, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. It is better for you to help us from the city."
The king said to them, "I will do what seems best to you." So the king stood by the gate. All the people went out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king told Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, "Be gentle with the young man Absalom, for my sake." All the people heard the king say this about Absalom.
The army went out to fight Israel. The battle was in the forest of Ephraim.
The men of Israel lost to David's servants there. That day many people died. Twenty thousand men died.
The battle spread over the whole land. That day the forest killed more people than the sword did.

Absalom met David's servants. He was riding a mule. The mule went under the thick branches of a big oak tree. Absalom's head got stuck in the oak. The mule kept going. So he hung between the sky and the ground.
A man saw it and told Joab. He said, "I saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree."
Joab said to the man who told him, "You saw him? Why didn't you strike him to the ground? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a belt."
The man said to Joab, "Even if I had a thousand pieces of silver in my hand, I would not hurt the king's son. We heard the king tell you, Abishai, and Ittai, 'Watch over the young man Absalom.'"
"If I had killed him, it would not have stayed hidden from the king. And you would have turned against me."
Joab said, "I will not wait here with you." He took three sharp sticks in his hand and stabbed them into Absalom's heart while he was still alive in the oak.
Ten young men who carried Joab's weapons came around Absalom and hit him and killed him.
Joab blew the trumpet. The people stopped chasing Israel. Joab held back the people.
They took Absalom and threw him into a big hole in the forest. They piled a very big heap of stones over him. Then all Israel ran away, each to his own tent.

While he was alive, Absalom had set up a stone pillar for himself in the King's Valley. He said, "I have no son to keep my name alive." He named the pillar after himself. It is called Absalom's pillar to this day.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Let me run and tell the king the good news. The LORD has saved him from his enemies."
Joab said to him, "You are not the man to bring news today. You may bring news another day. But today you must not bring news, because the king's son is dead."
Joab said to the Cushite, "Go tell the king what you saw." The Cushite bowed to Joab and ran.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Whatever happens, let me run too, after the Cushite." Joab said, "Why do you want to run, my son? You will not get a reward for this news."
Ahimaaz said, "But let me run." So Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain. He passed the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall. He looked up and saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he brings good news." The man kept coming closer.

The watchman saw another man running alone. He called to the gatekeeper and said, "Look, another man is running alone. This one is also bringing good news." The king said, "This one also brings good news."
The watchman said, "I think the first runner is Ahimaaz son of Zadok." The king said, "He is a good man. He comes with good news."

Ahimaaz called out to the king, "Peace!" He bowed down to the ground before the king. He said, "Praise the LORD your God! He has given you the win over the men who lifted their hands against my lord the king."
The king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz said, "When Joab sent your servant, I saw a big crowd. But I did not know what it was."
The king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he stood there.
Then the Cushite came. He said, "My lord the king, good news! The LORD has saved you today from all who rose up against you."
The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" The Cushite said, "May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you to do harm, be like that young man."
The king was very upset. He went up to the room over the gate and cried. As he went, he said, "My son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! I wish I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son, my son!"
Someone told Joab, "The king is crying and mourning for Absalom."
The army's win that day became sad for everyone, because the people heard the king was sad about his son.
The people sneaked back into the city that day, like people sneak away in shame when they run from a battle.
The king hid his face and cried out loud, "Oh, my son Absalom! Oh, Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab went to the king in his house and said, "Today you made all your servants feel ashamed. They saved your life today, and the lives of your sons, daughters, wives, and other wives.

You love people who hate you, and you hate people who love you. Today you showed that your leaders and servants mean nothing to you. Today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, you would be happy.

Now get up and go out. Speak kindly to your servants. I swear by the LORD, if you do not go out, not one man will stay with you tonight. That would be worse for you than all the trouble you have had since you were young."
The king got up and sat in the gate. People were told, "The king is sitting in the gate." Then all the people came before the king. By then, Israel's soldiers had run away, each to his own tent.
All the people in all the tribes of Israel were arguing. They said, "The king saved us from our enemies. He saved us from the Philistines. But now he ran from the country because of Absalom.
Absalom, the one we chose to be over us, died in battle. So why are you not talking about bringing the king back?"

King David sent a message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. He said, "Speak to the elders of Judah. Ask them, 'Why are you the last to bring the king back to his house? The words of all Israel have reached the king about bringing him to his house.
You are my brothers, my own flesh and bone. Why are you the last to bring back the king?'
Also say to Amasa, 'Are you not my flesh and bone? May God punish me if you are not the commander of my army from now on instead of Joab.'"
David won over the hearts of all the men of Judah. They became like one man. They sent a message to the king: "Come back, you and all your servants."
The king came back and reached the Jordan. The people of Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and help him cross the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, a man from Benjamin's family from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand men from Benjamin were with him. Ziba, who had served Saul's family, was there too, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed to the Jordan ahead of the king.
They crossed the river to help the king's family cross and to do what pleased him. Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king as he crossed the Jordan.
Shimei said to the king, "My lord, please do not blame me. Do not remember the wrong your servant did on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Please do not take it to heart.
I know I have sinned. That is why I came today, the first of all Joseph's family, to meet my lord the king."
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, "Should Shimei not be put to death for this? He cursed the LORD's anointed one."
David said, "What do you and I have in common, sons of Zeruiah? Why are you against me today? Should any man be killed in Israel today? Do I not know that today I am king over Israel?"
The king said to Shimei, "You will not die." The king swore to him.
Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet, trimmed his mustache, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he came back safely.
When he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"
Mephibosheth answered, "My lord the king, my servant tricked me. Your servant said, 'I will saddle the donkey and ride with the king,' because your servant is lame.
He has lied about your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like an angel of God. Do what seems good to you.
All my father's family were as good as dead before my lord the king. Yet you let your servant eat at your table. What right do I have to ask the king for more?"
The king said, "Why talk more? I say you and Ziba will share the field."
Mephibosheth said, "Let him take it all, since my lord the king has come home safely."
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim. He crossed the Jordan with the king to send him on his way.
Barzillai was very old. He was eighty years old. He had fed the king while the king stayed at Mahanaim, because he was a very rich man.
The king said to Barzillai, "Cross over with me. I will take care of you in Jerusalem."
Barzillai said to the king, "How many years do I have left to live? Why should I go up with the king to Jerusalem?
I am eighty years old today. Can I tell good from bad? Can your servant taste what I eat or drink? Can I still hear men and women sing? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king reward me with all this?

Please let your servant go back. I want to die in my own city, near my father's and mother's graves. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him cross over with my lord the king. Do for him what seems good to you."
The king said, "Chimham will cross with me. I will do for him what seems good to you. I will do for you whatever you ask."
All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed too. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him. Then Barzillai went back home.
The king went on to Gilgal. Chimham went with him. All the people of Judah and half the people of Israel brought the king across.
Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said, "Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, steal you away? They brought the king and his family across the Jordan, along with all David's men."
The men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "The king is our close relative. Why are you angry about this? Have we eaten at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?"

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king. We have more claim on David than you do. Why did you look down on us? Were we not the first to talk about bringing our king back?" But the words of the men of Judah were stronger than the words of the men of Israel.
A troublemaker named Sheba son of Bichri was from Benjamin. He blew a trumpet and said, "We have no part with David. We have no share with Jesse's son. Everyone, go to your own homes, Israel!"
So all the men of Israel left David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed with their king from the Jordan River to Jerusalem.

David came to his house in Jerusalem. The king took the ten women he had left to watch the house. He put them in a guarded house. He gave them food, but he did not sleep with them. They stayed there like widows until they died.
The king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah to me in three days. Be here yourself."
Amasa went to call Judah together. But he took longer than the time David had set.
David said to Abishai, "Sheba son of Bichri will hurt us more than Absalom did. Take your lord's men and chase him. If he finds a strong city, he may hide there and get away from us."
Joab's men went with him. The Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the brave men went too. They left Jerusalem to chase Sheba son of Bichri.
They were at the big stone in Gibeon when Amasa met them. Joab had his armor on. He had a sword in its case on his belt. As he stepped forward, the sword fell out.
Joab said to Amasa, "Are you okay, my brother?" Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

Amasa did not watch the sword in Joab's hand. Joab struck him in the stomach. His insides spilled on the ground. Joab did not strike him again. Amasa died. Then Joab and Abishai chased Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young helpers stood by Amasa and said, "Whoever is for Joab, and whoever is for David, follow Joab!"
Amasa was lying in his blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that all the people were stopping, he dragged Amasa off the road into a field. He threw a cloth over him.
When Amasa was moved off the road, everyone went on after Joab to chase Sheba son of Bichri.
Sheba went through all the tribes of Israel to Abel Beth Maacah. The people of Beri gathered and followed him too.
Joab's men came and trapped him in Abel Beth Maacah. They piled dirt up to the city wall. The wall stood firm. All the people with Joab worked to knock the wall down.
A wise woman called from the city, "Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here. I want to talk to you."
Joab came near her. The woman asked, "Are you Joab?" He said, "I am." She said, "Listen to your servant." He said, "I am listening."
She said, "In the old days people said, 'Ask advice at Abel,' and that settled things."
She said, "I am one of the peaceful, faithful people of Israel. You are trying to destroy a city that is important in Israel. Why would you destroy what belongs to the LORD?"
Joab said, "No! I do not want to destroy or ruin anything!"

He said, "That is not it. A man named Sheba son of Bichri is from the hills of Ephraim. He has rebelled against King David. Hand him over, and I will leave the city." The woman said to Joab, "His head will be thrown to you over the wall."

The woman went to all the people with her wise words. They cut off Sheba's head and threw it to Joab. He blew the trumpet. The men left the city and went home. Joab went back to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab was over all the army of Israel. Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites.
Adoram was over the forced work. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the record keeper.
Sheva was the writer. Zadok and Abiathar were the priests.
Ira the Jairite was also a priest for David.
During David’s rule, there was no food for three years in a row. David asked the the LORD for help. The The LORD said, “This is because of Saul and his family. They killed the Gibeonites.”

The king called the Gibeonites and talked with them. The Gibeonites were not Israelites. They were part of the Amorites who were left. Israel had promised to let them live. But Saul tried to kill them to help Israel and Judah.
David said to the Gibeonites, “What can I do for you? How can I make this right so you will bless the LORD’s land?”
The Gibeonites said, “We do not want silver or gold from Saul or his family. We also cannot kill anyone in Israel.” Then David asked, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said, “The man who hurt us and tried to wipe us out kept us from living in Israel.”
“Give us seven men from his family. We will hang them before the the LORD in Gibeah, Saul’s town. Saul was the man the LORD chose.” The king said, “I will give them to you.”
But the king saved Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul. He kept him safe because of the promise before the the LORD between David and Jonathan, son of Saul.

Instead, the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth. These were the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had for Saul. He also took the five sons of Merab daughter of Saul. Merab had these sons with Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.
He gave them to the Gibeonites. They hanged them on a hill before the the LORD. All seven died together. They were killed at the start of the harvest, when the barley was ready.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah took rough cloth and spread it on a rock for herself. She stayed there from the start of the harvest until rain fell from the sky. She did not let birds land on the bodies during the day. She did not let wild animals come near at night.
David heard what Rizpah, a wife of Saul, had done.

David went and took the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh Gilead. These men had taken the bones from the town square in Beth Shan. The Philistines had hung the bodies there when they killed Saul at Gilboa.
David brought the bones of Saul and Jonathan from there. The people also gathered the bones of the men who had been hanged.

They buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan in Zela, in Benjamin’s land. They put them in the tomb of Saul’s father, Kish. After they did all the king said, God heard their prayers and helped the land.
Later, the Philistines fought Israel again. David and his men went to fight. David got very tired.
Ishbi-Benob was from Rapha’s family. He had a heavy bronze spear and a new sword. He tried to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah helped David. He hit the Philistine and killed him. Then David’s men made a promise. They said, “You must not go out to battle with us again. We do not want Israel’s light to go out.”
Later, there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, who was from Rapha’s family.
There was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. Elhanan son of Jaare-Oregim from Bethlehem killed Goliath the Gittite. Goliath’s spear was as big as a heavy wooden beam.
There was another battle at Gath. There was a very tall man there. He had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. That is 24 in all. He was from Rapha’s family.
When he made fun of Israel, Jonathan, the son of David’s brother Shimei, killed him.
These four men from Rapha’s family in Gath were killed by David and his men.
David sang to the LORD the words of this song when the LORD had saved him from all his enemies and from Saul.
"The LORD is my rock, my safe place, and my rescuer.
My God is my rock. I hide in Him. He is my shield and the power that saves me. He is my strong place and my safe place. He saves me from being hurt.
I will call on the LORD. He should be praised. He saves me from my enemies.
"The waves of death came over me. Floods of trouble scared me.
The ropes of the grave held me. The traps of death came to get me.
When I was in trouble, I called to the LORD. I cried to my God. He heard my voice from His temple. My cry for help reached His ears.
"The earth shook and moved. The base of the sky shook. They shook because He was angry.
Smoke came from His nose. Fire came from His mouth and burned. Hot coals blazed.
He pushed the sky aside and came down. Dark clouds were under His feet.
He rode on a winged angel and flew. He soared on the wings of the wind.
He made darkness His tent. Dark clouds and water gathered around Him.
From His bright light, burning coals blazed.
The LORD thundered from heaven. The Most High sent out His voice.
He shot arrows and scattered them. He sent lightning and chased them away.
